stories.title: Uganda: Slow Poison - Idi Amin, Yoweri Museveni, and the Making of the Ugandan State
stories.summary: Uganda: Slow Poison - Idi Amin, Yoweri Museveni, and the Making of the Ugandan State Supplied Slow Poison: Idi Amin, Yoweri Museveni, and the Making of the Ugandan State By Mahmood Mamdani 27 October 2026 allAfrica.com book review By Uma Dhupelia-Mesthrie Slow Poison: Idi Amin, Yoweri Museveni, and the Making of the Ugandan State By Mahmood Mamdani Review by Uma Dhupelia-Mesthrie Wits University Press, 2025, 338 pp., R380 The two protagonists of this book are Idi Amin, president of Uganda between 1971 and 1979, and Yoweri Museveni, the president from 1986 until now. Drawing on rich official and unofficial archival sources, including an unpublished biography of Amin by his son Jaffar, Mamdani provides a background to their lives before assuming the presidency, with insights into their personalities. The main focus though is on their terms as presidents and their legacy. Mamdani’s assessment of Amin unsettles dominant public images of Amin, which became well established through a 1981 film, The Rise and Fall of Idi Amin , and which continued in the western media well into the 21st century. While he concedes that violence was a key part of Amin’s life and strategy to win power, he debunks the image of Amin as a cannibal, a man who kept severed heads of people in his fridge, who sacrificed his son and who was a monster equal to Hitler.

stories.title: Kenya: Cyber Threats in Kenya Rise 14.45pc to 2.6 Billion in Q3
stories.summary: Kenya: Cyber Threats in Kenya Rise 14.45pc to 2.6 Billion in Q3 27 October 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Kevin Rotich Nairobi — Kenya recorded 2.6 billion cyber threat events in the three months to September 2026, a 14.45 percent increase from the previous quarter, according to the Communications Authority of Kenya (CA). The regulator attributed the rise to inadequate system updates, limited public awareness of phishing and other social engineering attacks, and the growing use of artificial intelligence by criminals to carry out more sophisticated attacks. System attacks accounted for the largest share of detected threats at 2.55 billion, followed by malware at 8.37 million, brute-force attacks at 916,418 and web attacks at 549,931. The report also recorded 18,837 mobile application attacks, 13,201 distributed denial-of-service attacks and 112 other attack events. In response, the National Kenya Computer Incident Response Team Coordination Centre (National KE-CIRT/CC) issued 20.3 million cyber threat advisories between July and September 2026, a 2.36 percent decline from the number issued in the April-to-June period.

stories.title: Ethiopia: Drought, Food Shortages and Child Malnutrition Deepen Humanitarian Needs in Afar, Amhara and Tigray
stories.summary: Ethiopia: Drought, Food Shortages and Child Malnutrition Deepen Humanitarian Needs in Afar, Amhara and Tigray World Food Programme South Omo zone in Ethiopia is facing a severe drought (file photo) 27 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Drought, rising food prices, shortages of essential medicines and disruptions to health services are compounding humanitarian needs across northern Ethiopia's Afar , Amhara and Tigray regions , with displaced children particularly vulnerable to acute malnutrition, according to a humanitarian assessment document seen by Addis Standard. The assessment, dated October 19 and covering developments between October 12 and 19, warns that the humanitarian consequences of escalating insecurity are unfolding against a backdrop of unmet needs left by the 2020-2022 northern Ethiopia conflict, subsequent episodes of fighting and displacement, and El Niño-related drought. "Needs are likely to remain high," the assessment states, noting that the combined pressures have compounded existing humanitarian vulnerabilities across Tigray, Amhara and Afar. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn One of the clearest indicators of the crisis is the nutritional situation among displaced children in Tigray. Screening conducted in September and October in Laelay Adiabo, Axum and Adwa found that approximately 15% of around 11,800 children screened in internally displaced communities had moderate acute malnutrition. The assessment cautions that information on the overall scale and severity of humanitarian needs remains fragmented. "At the time of writing, there is no needs assessment data available," it states, identifying rapid humanitarian needs assessments as a priority as access improves.

stories.summary: Paddy Donnelly came to London from South Africa in the early 80s to work for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa View image in fullscreen Paddy Donnelly came to London from South Africa in the early 80s to work for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa Obituary Paddy Donnelly obituary My husband, Paddy Donnelly, who has died aged 70, was a South African who moved in the early 1980s to London. There he worked for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa (IDAF), which funded the legal costs of people tried or imprisoned for anti-apartheid activity. In addition to its legal work, the IDAF had a large archive of photographs relating to apartheid, and Paddy ran that side of the operation, processing and distributing photos of ongoing state violence to media outlets, campaigning groups and many other organisations. He was an accomplished photographer himself, and many of his photos were held in the archive. He had begun by taking pictures of townships and displaced people’s camps, and when he came to the UK he photographed anti-apartheid political meetings as well as visiting or exiled South African singers, musicians and activists.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.” The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week. The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation. “The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.

stories.title: 'Tinubu Must Go!': Nigeria's northern protests test limits of political dissent
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5OTCD Police said the men were found in possession of 'dried leaves,' a pair of scissors and T-shirts bearing the phrase 'Tinubu Must Go!' Image: Borno State Police Command Advertisement T-shirts bearing the slogan "Tinubu Must Go!" — a reference to Nigerian President Bola Tinubu — are at the center of an escalating crackdown on dissent in Nigeria 's vast north. In September, police in the northeastern state of Borno arrested five men, aged between 21 and 44, over the shirts. Authorities have alleged the group had conspired to produce and wear them with the intention of breaching public peace. The men were subsequently charged with criminal conspiracy, inciting disturbance, disturbance of public peace and thuggery. Drawing criticism from human rights groups and activists, police later explained that the arrests followed a routine patrol and that officers had found substances believed to be illicit drugs and other items on the men, arguing that they were not being prosecuted for expressing their political views.
